planting.note: Plant in spring or early fall with roots shaded and cool, giving the twining stems a low fence, shrub, or wire support to climb through.

directions: A Korean species in the same bell-flowered Atragene group as C. alpina and C. macropetala, this clematis opens nodding, lantern-shaped flowers in shades of purple, pink, or yellow-green in spring on the previous year's growth. It has become an important parent species behind many modern compact nodding-bell garden hybrids. Grow it over a low trellis, shrub, or fence with its roots kept cool and shaded, and prune only lightly right after flowering to remove dead wood, since hard pruning would remove the coming season's buds.

planting.note: Plant in spring with roots shaded and cool, giving the fine twining stems a low fence, obelisk, or shrub support.

directions: Another Korean species in the bell-flowered Atragene group, this clematis bears nodding, narrow, lantern-shaped yellow to yellow-green flowers in late spring, often with a faint reddish flush on the outer tepals, followed by fluffy seed heads. Like its relatives C. alpina and C. koreana it flowers on the previous year's growth, so prune only lightly right after bloom to remove dead wood. Its modest scale suits a rock garden, low trellis, or mixed border rather than a large structure.

planting.note: Plant in spring or early fall with the crown a couple of inches below soil level and roots shaded, giving it a fence, trellis, or wire support to climb.

directions: A Japanese species that, along with C. lanuginosa, stands behind most of the large-flowered garden hybrids grown today (the Patens Group of early, large single-flowered cultivars). It opens broad, flat, pale lavender to violet flowers with prominent central tepals in late spring on the previous year's growth, followed by a lighter repeat flush later in summer on new wood. Grow it with roots shaded and cool against a fence, wall, or obelisk, and prune only lightly after the first flush to avoid removing next year's buds.

planting.note: Plant in spring with roots shaded and cool, giving it a sturdy fence, trellis, or wall to climb.

directions: A Chinese species named for the soft down covering its young leaves and stems, this clematis bears large, pale lavender-blue flowers with woolly grey-green sepal reverses in early to midsummer. It is one of the key ancestor species behind the large-flowered hybrid clematis grown widely today, prized historically for the exceptional size of its blooms. Grow it against a fence or trellis with roots kept cool and shaded, and prune lightly to shape rather than cutting hard, since flowering occurs on both old and new wood depending on the season.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained, rocky or shaley soil in spring; this species comes from thin, alkaline Appalachian substrates and resents heavy, wet ground.

directions: A rare, non-climbing native of shale barrens and rocky outcrops in Virginia and West Virginia, named for the dense whitish down covering its young growth and the outside of its urn-shaped, thick-textured purple-brown flowers. Like its relatives C. ochroleuca and C. viticaulis, it belongs to the leatherflower (Viorna) group and forms a low, non-vining clump rather than climbing. Grow it in lean, sharply drained, rocky soil in full sun and avoid summer irrigation, since it is adapted to droughty, thin-soiled sites.
sources: North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant in lean, well-drained soil in spring; this dryland native dislikes rich, consistently moist garden beds.

directions: A low, non-climbing native of sagebrush steppe and dry grasslands of the Pacific Northwest and Rocky Mountain region, commonly called sugarbowls for its thick, nodding, urn-shaped purple-blue flowers held just above silvery, finely divided foliage in spring. Like other members of the Viorna group it does not climb and is best used as a drought-tolerant groundcover or rock-garden plant in lean, fast-draining soil. It goes dormant and dislikes summer irrigation once established, making it a good match for xeric plantings.

planting.note: Plant in a sheltered, mild-winter site in spring, giving it a substantial tree, arbor, or wall to scramble into.

directions: A vigorous climbing species from the Himalayan foothills of Nepal, Pakistan, and northern India, bearing airy, branched clusters of small, fragrant white flowers in late summer and fall followed by silky seed heads. It is considerably more tender than the familiar East Asian and European garden clematis and performs best where winters stay mild. Give it a large tree, arbor, or wall to climb into, since it can grow rampantly in a single season once established.

planting.note: Plant in a sheltered, mild-winter site in spring, giving it a sturdy tree, arbor, or wall support.

directions: A Himalayan climbing species from Nepal and western China with downy, deeply veined foliage and nodding clusters of small, bell-shaped, pale yellow to greenish flowers in late summer and fall, followed by fluffy seed heads. It is more cold-tender than common garden clematis and best suited to mild-winter regions. Grow it into a large shrub, tree, or sturdy arbor, since it is a vigorous grower once established in a sheltered site.

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall with roots cool and shaded, giving it a trellis, obelisk, or large container support.

directions: A compact, free-flowering large-flowered cultivar bearing deep wine-red flowers with a velvety sheen through summer. Its more restrained habit compared to older large-flowered hybrids suits a medium trellis, obelisk, or large container as readily as a border. Grow with roots shaded and cool in full sun, and prune back in late winter to a healthy pair of buds since it flowers on the current season's growth.

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall with roots cool and shaded, giving it a fence, trellis, or arbor to climb.

directions: A classic large-flowered English cultivar bearing rich purple-blue flowers with a slightly deeper central bar and reddish anthers, opening in late spring with a lighter repeat flush in late summer. Grow against a fence, trellis, or arbor with roots shaded and cool, and prune lightly after the first flush, removing only weak or dead stems, since the main flush comes on the previous year's growth.

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall with roots cool and shaded, giving it a fence, trellis, or arbor to climb.

directions: A large-flowered cultivar bearing pure white flowers with a faint central bar and contrasting dark red anthers, opening in late spring on the previous year's growth with a lighter repeat flush later in summer on new growth. Grow against a fence, trellis, or arbor with roots shaded and cool, and prune only lightly after the first flush to avoid removing next year's buds.

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall with roots cool and shaded, weaving the lax stems through a trellis or shrub support.

directions: A Polish-raised viticella-group cultivar producing abundant, deep velvety purple-black flowers with a near-black sheen from midsummer into fall, among the darkest of the viticella cultivars. Like other members of the group it flowers entirely on the current season's growth, so cut the whole plant back hard to a low pair of buds in late winter. Its vigorous, free-flowering habit suits a trellis, arbor, or large shrub to scramble through.

planting.note: Plant in spring or fall with roots cool and shaded, weaving the lax stems through a trellis or shrub support.

directions: A Dutch-raised viticella-group cultivar bearing nodding, rich wine-red to plum-purple flowers from midsummer into fall. It flowers entirely on the current season's growth, so cut the whole plant back hard to a low pair of buds in late winter. Its free-flowering, lax habit makes it a good choice for weaving through a trellis, shrub, or small tree rather than relying on it to self-cling.

planting.note: Plant in spring with roots cool and shaded, letting the lax stems weave through nearby perennials or a low support.

directions: A cold-hardy Canadian-raised hybrid between C. integrifolia and C. viticella, sharing the sprawling, non-clinging habit of its integrifolia parent while adding viticella vigor. It bears nodding, bell-shaped mid-blue flowers with recurved tepal tips from midsummer into fall on lax stems best woven through a low trellis or sturdy border companions. Cut the whole plant back hard in late winter, since it flowers on growth produced the same season.
